Khayelitsha Extortion

By: Catherine Rice | Commission

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Extortion has become an increasingly sinister enterprise in Cape Town, spreading its tentacles from the city to the sprawling townships on its outskirts.

Unique Selling Point:
A Khayelitsha pastor speaks out about the targeting of churches by the foot soldiers of extortion gangs, and how it has become impossible to keep his congregation safe. From braai meat sellers on the street to business owners, nobody is untouchable as gangs infiltrate at every level demanding protection fees.

Summary:
Extortion rackets have spread their tentacles, demanding protection fees from businesses, spaza shops, salons and even informal street traders. On June 8, a barbershop in Site C, Khayelitsha was attacked when gunmen stormed the salon. Three children, aged 4, 11 and 12 died in the attack. A fourth person, a thirty year old was also murdered. Nine people were seriously injured. It's possible that protection rackets are behind the brutal attack. Two men were arrested and appeared in the Khayelitsha Magistrate's Court, where we were able to film proceedings. Fear stalks Khayelitsha residents, nobody is safe in this sprawling township, where refusing to pay these criminal syndicates comes with a price. Mass shootings linked to extortion have become commonplace.

Script:


VO 1 A Saturday afternoon in Khayelitsha outside Cape Town. Children play in the streets. But, in an instant, joy turns to terror as four gunmen open fire on a local barbershop.

NATSOUND SHEILA: Her mummy just come out calling Enzo Enzo Enzo. When she came here, I notice no man there’s blood the whole body of Enzo.

VO 2 In a township of more than two million people, the daily grind has taken a sinister turn.

VO 3 Where gangs unleash appalling violence on people unwilling or unable to pay for their protection. Where a courageous few risk their lives standing up to the intimidation and threats.

NATSOUND

UPSOUND Monde Bambelo / Khayelitsha CPF Chairperson: This area here, this is where most of the gangs reside.

VO 4 Monde Bambelo, chairperson of the Khayelitsha Community Policing Forum, is taking us on a tour … of a different kind.

UPSOUND Monde Bambelo: Upstairs on my right, a massacre of nine people here, even back then, it has always been extortion related.

VO 5 Mass shootings linked to extortion have become a regular occurrence in this area. .

UPSOUND Monde Bambelo: Now we are here by Amazizi where the other massacre happened where six people were gunned down. From Saps, from the community, everyone agrees that all these crimes that are happening, all these mass shootings are all linked or related to extortion.

VO 6 Rival gangs fight for control of areas, demanding protection fees from formal and informal businesses. Pay up, and your business will be protected. Refuse and face the consequences.

UPSOUND Monde Bambelo: They find a common ground, these gangs, and team up together to actually make money. The incident happened in this street, five guys gunned down, they all died.
GOVAN: Is it unsafe to stop here?
Monde: Yep, we’re not safe even in this car. They just pull up next to you. People get out of the car, start shooting at you. It’s not just about outsiders anymore. No one is safe.

LINK In recent years, extortion rackets have exploded into every sector of business in Khayelitsha. Even street vendors like these are being forced to pay protection fees.

VO 7 Somalian owned businesses were historically the target of extortion gangs. But, in recent years, that’s changed, expanding to locals too.

UPSOUND Jenni Irish-Qhobosheane / Global Initiative Against Transnational Organised Crime: Particularly after Covid 19, it was very lucrative, and it then spread to local businesses..

VO 8 Jenni Irish-Qhobosheane is a senior analyst at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organised Crime - and she believes township extortion isn’t getting enough attention.

UPSOUND Jenni Irish-Qhobosheane: You see people who have been involved in armed robberies, cash and transit heists moving into the extortion economy. One because its’ a lucrative economy, but two it’s a lower risk economy. So if you cash in transit heist, you’re going up against armed security, quite a dangerous job, but extorting someone you just need to have a gun and the person you’re extorting is unlikely to be armed.

LINK Mass shootings have become commonplace here in Khayelitsha. In 2022, an alleged extortion kingpin known as “Bara” was arrested and accused of using violence to extort informal businesses.

VO 9 The arrest of Yanga Nyalara, known as “Bara” was seen as a breakthrough in combatting the wave of mass shootings in Khayelitsha. He faces 12 counts of murder allegedly linked to extortion. This week, his trial, along with one co-accused, started in a prison court because of security risks. Both men pleaded not guilty. Two witnesses in the case have already been murdered.

VO 10 Some in the community have rallied behind “Bara” because he allegedly targeted foreign owned businesses and not South Africans.

UPSOUND Monde Bambelo: Others want to do extortion to almost everyone, others are saying no they can do protection fees only to foreign nationals, and that creates a conflict amongst themselves. Community rallies behind the likes of Bara because Bara from time to time were to say the people from where we stay shouldn’t be robbed.

VO 11 Just a few weeks ago, this barbershop in Site C was targeted. A man….and three children…were shot dead. The youngest…four year old Enzokhule Dladlu.

NATSOUND Sheila: As it always they are just playing here.
GOVAN: Oh the kids play here on the main road.
Sheila: Ja, and then the shooting was happening here.
Sheila: After twenty bullets, dooof doof doof, it was not stopping just continuing continuing.

VO 12 Enzokuhle was not even at the barber shop. She was playing in the street outside, less than a hundred meters from her home.

VO 13 Her grandmother Sheila lives with Enzo’s mother who was too devastated to talk to us.

UPSOUND Sheila Dladlu / Grandmother: Every night I just wake up at 2 o’clock thinking about it.

NATSOUND CRYING
GOVAN: Your daughter’s crying again. Oh mama, its still fresh.

VO 14 Enzokuhle was her only child.

VO 15 The family hasn’t received any counselling from social services.

LINK: In the aftermath, the police picked up twenty eight cartridges and three bullets. And while the motive remains unclear for now, the NPA haven’t ruled out adding extortion charges in the case against two men they’ve arrested.

VO 16 They appeared in the Khayelitsha Magistrate’s Court earlier this month for a bail application - the media wasn’t allowed to film their faces because there are still ID parades to be done. They’re facing a range of charges including four counts of murder, eleven of attempted murder, and the illegal possession of firearms.

VO 17 But small businesses aren’t the only targets. Astonishingly, the extortion scourge has even spread to churches. A local pastor who agreed to talk to us, as long as we didn’t show his face, says his church has been targeted several times.

UPSOUND Pastor: Church before it was a safe place but not these days. Time code 01:26 They can just come in and take everything, and take it out to sell.. Besides that they can come tonight taking everything in your church
GOVAN: How often do they come in a month?
UPSOUND Pastor: It depend. Because there are a lot of churches here in Khayelitsha. This is happening every day my brother.

UPSOUND Jenni Irish Qhobasheane: Churches have always been a little bit of ground that nobody really wants to touch. But, I think we’re seeing the ruthlessness of the kind of gangs that are developing in the areas where nothing is sacrosanct.
GOVAN: Are these the same gangs that are extorting people?
UPSOUND Jenni: Some of them would be, but you would find some of the smaller gangs that operate with the blessing of the bigger gangs that would be involved in those sorts of activities.
GOVAN: But, it’s not as formalised as the extortion that’s happening in the city centre where they giving out invoices, right?
UPSOUND Jenni: It’s not as sophisticated. So what you see in the city centre is very classic kind of protection racketeering that you see in other places in the world. Where businesses are being told pay us, we’ll provide the security and doormen for your businesses, and if you refuse to employ their security company, then you will face the consequences. In Khayelitsha, that service isn’t even being provided, you just pay for them to actually protect you and you’re actually protecting yourself against them.

UPSOUND Monde Bambelo: I’ve heard a saloon where they say they pay R150, others they pay R300, others they pay up to R1000.

VO 18 Monde is fighting back and is even prepared to face down the extortionists to help reclaim his community.

UPSOUND Monde Bambelo: If I can convince one of them to understand the type of life they are putting us through, at least there’s a victory there. We have this problem, but let’s talk, but how do we get out of it?

PAUSE

VO 19 And the consequences of not getting out of it are borne by people like these seemingly carefree children…living in a place where the innocent are often caught in the crossfire.

UPSOUND Sheila Dladlu / Grandmother: You raise the child, you don’t know what is going to happen. We are so traumatised. Maybe it’s the end of the world.
